chicken-drumstick-baked-or-broiled-skin-.title: Chicken drumstick, baked or broiled, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken drumsticks are the meat from the lower leg of a chicken, commonly prepared by baking or broiling. In this version the skin is not eaten and the product is pre‑cooked (code 804). The meat is tender, provides high‑quality protein, B‑vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks are a staple in many cuisines, from American BBQ to Asian soups.
Baking without skin reduces fat content while retaining juiciness from the meat’s natural juices.
Poultry is one of the most affordable complete protein sources.
Pre‑cooking (code 804) shortens home cooking time.
Drumsticks are rich in collagen, beneficial for skin and joint health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 20 g of complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bone health, immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Low fat when skin‑less
items.content: Removing the skin cuts saturated fat, making the dish more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: Protein and a modest amount of fat help keep you feeling full longer, useful for weight management.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave salmonella or campylobacter; ensure the product is thoroughly heated.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Pre‑cooked items may contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some ready‑made products include preservatives or flavor enhancers that may not suit everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat drumsticks in the oven, microwave or skillet. They work well added to salads, soups, rice or pasta dishes, and can be enjoyed as a protein‑rich snack. Remove the skin before eating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the pre‑cooked product refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for 2‑3 months. Ensure it is fully reheated before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Lime juice is 100% freshly squeezed lime juice with no added sugar, preservatives, or water. It has a bright, tart flavor and the characteristic aroma of ripe limes, and is widely used in cooking, beverages, and cosmetics.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lime belongs to the citrus family and grows in tropical and subtropical regions.
A tablespoon (≈15 ml) of lime juice provides about 15 % of the daily recommended vitamin C.
Lime has been used in traditional medicine to aid digestion and as an antiseptic.
The acidity of lime juice can change the color of some foods, slowing the browning of avocado.
In several cultures lime is a symbol of hospitality and is used in welcoming rituals.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The acidity stimulates gastric juice production, helping to break down food.

items.title: Aids detoxification
items.content: Lime juice’s diuretic properties help the body eliminate toxins.

items.title: May reduce kidney stone risk
items.content: Citrus acids increase urinary citrate, which can inhibit formation of oxalate stones.

items.title: Improves skin health
items.content: Vitamin C and antioxidants combat signs of aging and promote healing of minor skin damage.

items.title: Acid reflux
items.content: People with high stomach acidity may experience increased heartburn after consuming lime juice.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may have an allergic reaction to lime.

items.title: Tooth enamel erosion
items.content: Frequent consumption of acidic drinks can wear down tooth enamel.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Lime acidity can affect the efficacy of certain drugs, such as anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add lime juice to cocktails, marinades, sauces, salads, and desserts. It is a key ingredient in guacamole, fish marinades, and as a refreshing addition to water or tea.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator in a tightly sealed bottle. Once opened, use within 5–7 days. Discard if the color, smell, or taste changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Mushrooms are the fruiting bodies of fungi and are eaten around the world. Common edible types include button mushrooms, cremini, portobello, oyster, and shiitake. They have an earthy, savory flavor and a meaty texture, and they are used in soups, sauces, stir-fries, and many other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mushrooms belong to the kingdom of fungi, not to plants or animals.
Mushrooms can produce vitamin D when exposed to ultraviolet light.
Thousands of mushroom species exist, but only some are safe to eat.
Mushrooms are around 90 percent water.
Mushrooms have been used in cooking and traditional practices for centuries in many cultures.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Mushrooms are very low in calories and fat and add flavor and volume to meals.

items.title: Provides B vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms contain riboflavin, niacin, and pantothenic acid, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Mushrooms provide selenium, potassium, and copper.

items.title: Source of vitamin D when UV-exposed
items.content: Mushrooms exposed to ultraviolet light can be a plant-based source of vitamin D.

items.title: Contains beneficial compounds
items.content: Mushrooms contain antioxidants such as ergothioneine and fibers such as beta-glucans.

items.title: Poisonous wild mushrooms
items.content: Some wild mushrooms are toxic and can cause severe illness or death. Never eat wild mushrooms unless an expert has identified them.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms or their spores.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Mushrooms contain fibers that may cause bloating or discomfort in sensitive individuals, especially in large amounts.

items.title: Raw mushrooms
items.content: Some mushrooms should not be eaten raw. Cooking improves digestibility and safety.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mushrooms can be sautéed, grilled, roasted, baked, or added to soups, sauces, omelets, pizzas, and stir-fries. They are also used as fillings and in vegetarian dishes. Cook them thoroughly and buy them only from reliable sources.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh mushrooms in the refrigerator in a paper bag or a container lined with paper towels, which helps absorb moisture. Avoid washing them until just before use. Fresh mushrooms usually keep for several days. Mushrooms can also be dried or cooked and then frozen.

content.title: About
content.content: Palak Paneer is a classic Indian dish consisting of soft cottage cheese (paneer) cooked with spinach (palak) in a fragrant blend of spices. The dish is rich in protein, calcium, and iron, offering a creamy taste with a mild earthy note from the spinach.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Palak Paneer is often served in Indian restaurants as a vegetarian alternative to meat dishes.
Traditionally, paneer is made from whole milk without rennet, making it suitable for vegetarians.
Spinach used in the dish is high in iron, and its absorption is enhanced by vitamin C present in the spices.
Typical recipes include tomato puree, ginger, garlic, and garam masala, giving the dish its characteristic aroma.
In some regions, toasted cashews are added for extra richness.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Paneer provides high‑quality plant‑based protein important for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium for bone health
items.content: The cheese contributes a significant amount of calcium, supporting bone density.

items.title: Iron and energy
items.content: Spinach supplies iron, which is essential for oxygen transport and energy production.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish contains vitamin B6 and folate, which aid metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Spices such as turmeric and cumin have anti‑inflammatory and antioxidant properties.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Paneer is made from milk, so people with lactose intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: When salt and soy sauce are added, the dish can become high in sodium, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Oxalates in spinach
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates that can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to dairy should avoid paneer.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Palak Paneer is served hot, typically with basmati rice, naan, or chapati. It can be rolled in flatbreads, used as a filling for wraps, or enjoyed as a standalone main course. Garnish with fresh cilantro or toasted cashews for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked Palak Paneer in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. It can be frozen for up to 2 months after cooling to room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Light Ranch dressing is a reduced‑fat version of the classic Ranch sauce, made with low‑fat yogurt, kefir or skim milk. It retains the creamy, garlicky, herbaceous flavor of traditional Ranch while delivering fewer calories and less fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ranch is the best‑selling salad dressing in the United States and is commonly used as a dip for vegetables and chicken wings.
The light version was introduced in the early 2000s to meet growing demand for lower‑calorie condiments.
Typical ingredients include yogurt, kefir, dill, garlic, onion powder, and spices, making it more protein‑rich than the original mayonnaise‑based recipe.
Unlike the classic sauce, the light variant often contains no added sugar.
Chefs frequently use Ranch as a base for creating new flavor blends.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: Light Ranch provides roughly 50‑70 kcal per 30 g serving, making it suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Higher protein
items.content: The yogurt/kefir base supplies about 2‑3 g of protein per serving, helping to promote satiety.

items.title: Calcium and probiotics
items.content: Dairy components deliver calcium and live cultures that support bone health and gut microbiota.

items.title: Reduced saturated fat
items.content: Compared with traditional Ranch, the light version contains minimal saturated fat, which is better for cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dairy base provides vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Contains dairy, so it may cause discomfort for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Those allergic to casein or whey should avoid this dressing.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some commercial versions are high in salt; individuals monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Preservatives and flavorings
items.content: Processed varieties may include additives that are not suitable for clean‑eating diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Light Ranch works well as a salad dressing, dip for carrots, celery, crackers, and as a sauce for baked chicken, fish, or fries. It can be drizzled on sandwiches, wraps, and burgers to add creaminess without excess calories.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 2‑4 °C in a sealed container. After opening, it typically lasts 7‑10 days. Discard if you notice off‑smells, discoloration, or mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Ravioli are small pasta parcels filled with a seasoned blend of beef, pork, or a mixture of both. They are served hot in a fragrant tomato sauce or meat sauce, making the dish hearty and flavorful.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ravioli originated in Italy and have been prepared for over 800 years.
There are more than 30 regional filling variations, ranging from classic meat to cheese and vegetable blends.
The tomatoes used in the sauce are often the sweet San Marzano variety.
Ravioli are traditionally served as a "primo" (first course) in an Italian meal.
In some regions, ravioli are shaped like a flower, with two half‑circles joined at the center.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef and pork contain heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B12, B6, and niacin support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that may reduce the risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: Moderate healthy fats
items.content: Lean meat provides monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain a lot of salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Fatty cuts of meat can raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The pasta dough contains wheat gluten, making the dish unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Ravioli are energy‑dense; portions should be moderated for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve ravioli hot, drizzled with tomato or meat sauce. Sprinkle with grated Parmesan, fresh basil, or oregano. They pair well with a light arugula salad dressed with olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry ravioli in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 6 months. Cooked ravioli last 2–3 days in the refrigerator and up to 2 months in the freezer.
